content:
# Semantic-Anchor Checkpoints + Verkle Provenance Gate: Edge Case Analysis

## Framing contract (read this first — most bugs come from violating it)

Three layers, three different notions of "match," and they must never be conflated:

1. **Semantic layer** — determines where a cut is *legal* (message boundaries, tool-roundtrip boundaries, immutable blob interiors). It governs anchor placement and provenance grouping.
2. **Syntactic layer** — determines whether KV reuse is *numerically valid*: exact token-ID sequence match, exact position base, exact model/conditioning version. Hash-equality only.
3. **Provenance layer** — determines whether reuse is *admissible*: lineage, permissions, liveness, residency.

**Core invariant:** a semantic similarity score may never gate KV reuse. Fuzzy/paraphrase matching at the reuse layer is silent corruption, not a feature. Semantic anchors say *where* you may cut; syntactic identity says *whether* you may reuse; the gate says *whether you're allowed*.

---

## A. Cache-identity failure modes (the silent-corruption class)

**A1. Positional mismatch under duplicate content.** Agent contexts are full of repeated boilerplate (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot blocks). Content-hash longest-match can bind to the wrong occurrence. KV entries embed RoPE rotations at their original absolute positions; reusing a prefix cached at offset 0 for a span now living at offset 4096 produces wrong attention everywhere downstream. Fix: checkpoint records carry `position_base`; gate checks it, not just content hash.

**A2. Middle insertions masquerading as suffix appends.** Retrieval injects a document at turn 12 of 30. Everything after is textually unchanged but positionally shifted. Naive systems treat this as append and reuse mismatched KV. Correct handling exists: for RoPE-family models, only K is rotated (V is not), and rotations compose additively per frequency pair, so cached K can be exactly re-rotated by Δ = position_delta via elementwise complex multiply — O(n·d_head), no recompute. With quantized K: dequant → rotate → requant, rewriting scale metadata. This is valid *only* for RoPE-family; forbidden for any architecture baking absolute positions into K/V. If you don't implement re-rotation, a middle edit forces re-prefill from the insertion point. Either way: the gate must detect the shape of the edit (common-prefix diff at token level) and route accordingly. Never silently classify a middle edit as a suffix edit.

**A3. Tokenizer seams.** Re-prefilling "the new suffix" standalone re-tokenizes it; BPE merges across the boundary yield different token IDs than whole-string tokenization (`" world"` ≠ `world` after `"Hello"`). Off-by-one seams corrupt meaning invisibly. Rules: operate on token IDs end-to-end; if any stage round-trips through text, re-align via common-prefix token diff extended backward through a merge window (±16 tokens, iterate until stable); continuation segments must be encoded with special-token addition disabled (no accidental second BOS). Byte-offset anchoring without token-alignment verification is a bug.

**A4. Chunked KV quantization grids.** With dynamic per-chunk KV quantization (chunk = 128 tokens), the last prefix chunk's scale factors depend on its member tokens only — but any boundary not snapped to the chunk grid leaves a partially-valid chunk. Reuse boundary snaps to the quantization chunk grid, or the last chunk is recomputed.

**A5. Conditioning inputs invisible to content hash.** Same tokens, different LoRA adapter, different steering vector, different rope-scaling config (YaRN bump mid-session), different kernel version with different numeric behavior → different correct KV. The checkpoint record must bind `{weights_or_adapter_hash, tokenizer_hash, rope_config_hash, kernel_impl_version, quant_scheme, position_base, content_hash, kv_fingerprint}`. Gate denies on any missing or mismatched field. Content match alone never admits.

**A6. Attention-architecture blindness.** Sliding-window layers make anchors deeper than the window useless; hybrid layers (every k-th global) have per-layer horizons. Effective reusable horizon = min over layer types unless you implement per-layer reuse boundaries (most stacks don't). Plus attention sinks: the first few tokens absorb disproportionate attention; compaction that deletes them degrades the model even though "everything is committed." Reserve the first ~4 tokens as an untouchable sink span; the gate flags any checkpoint whose lineage shows sink-span deletion.

**A7. Float fingerprint tyranny.** Committing an expected KV fingerprint and demanding bit-equality on later re-prefill (after eviction) guarantees invalidation storms from kernel nondeterminism (reduction-order variation across batch shapes). Validate via quantized-bucket equality or measured-jitter tolerance bands — never assumed-zero float equality.

---

## B. Edit-shape and lifecycle failure modes

**B1. Edits racing live decode.** Swapping KV under an in-flight forward pass = torn attention read. Edits apply only between decode steps; swap is copy-on-write/double-buffered. In-place mutation of a segment referenced by a live decode must never happen.

**B2. Eviction vs. anchor liveness.** Chain says anchor k is valid; pages are gone. Acceptable outcomes: honest `MISS_FALLBACK_RECOMPUTE`. Unacceptable: crash, partial-segment reuse (garbage attention), or reporting a checkpoint hit that didn't happen (corrupts every metric, bill, and audit built on it). Gate checks a committed residency bitmap before admission; telemetry distinguishes `HIT_EXACT` / `HIT_SHIFTED` (re-rotated) / `MISS_RECOMPUTE`, and downstream accounting consumes only honest labels. Pinning rule: never evict the deepest resident anchor of a live session.

**B3. Crash windows.** Ordering is strict: persist pages + residency bitmap → fsync → append chain leaf → publish/attest root. Recovery scans for leaves referencing non-resident pages and tombstones them (append-only tombstone, never mutation). Publishing a root that references unpersisted pages is the cardinal sin of this subsystem.

**B4. Rollback ≠ revival.** Undo rewinds a pointer to an old checkpoint — but sources may have been revoked since. Checkpoint existence is necessary, not sufficient: the gate re-checks ancestor-leaf liveness at admission. Amortize with a revocation epoch counter; verdicts cache per `(anchor_id, root_epoch, model_version)` and flush on epoch bump.

**B5. Degenerate suffixes.** Delete-everything-after-anchor-k is a legal edit with an empty suffix; the no-op path must still emit correct logits from the cached final position. Batched serving with left-padding: `position_base` reflects unpadded logical positions; mixing padded and unpacked reuse corrupts.

---

## C. Verkle chain / gate failure modes

**C1. Fail-open is fatal.** Missing root, bad signature, malformed witness, verification timeout ⇒ DENY ⇒ full re-prefill with fresh provenance capture. Any infrastructure error defaulting to "allow" converts the gate into decoration.

**C2. Root staleness and forked acceptance.** Lagging validators hold old roots; new checkpoints prove against newer ones. Handle via a pinned window of the last K verified roots; advance pins only through signed root attestations. Auto-updating roots without signature verification, or rejecting valid proofs without triggering catch-up, are both failure modes.

**C3. Quadratic reverification.** Re-verifying from genesis per edit is quadratic over session length. Verify incrementally: each new checkpoint's proof links to the previously verified root; per-edit cost stays O(1). Caching "already verified" must be keyed by `(root_hash, epoch)` — an unkeyed memo is a forgery channel after a root change.

**C4. Key-schema conflicts.** Sequential-index keys make concurrent checkpoint creation (two workers building anchor k+1 from different suffixes) a conflict requiring resolution protocol. Content-addressed keys (`H(domain ‖ content_hash)`) make inserts idempotent and order-independent — including the benign case of identical contexts reached via different paths. Domain-separate the hash; never truncate below collision-resistance needs (≥128-bit security; 256-bit hashes, full-width keys). A 64-bit prefix ID in a gate that adversaries can feed tool-output text into is grindable.

**C5. Append-only leaves.** Overwriting a leaf value in place destroys the ability to reproduce past gate decisions ("prove this answer cited document D as it existed at t"). Versioned leaves (`key = H(content, seq)`), separate storage pruning from commitment structure.

**C6. Spec-version mixing.** Verkle key/layout spec bumps invalidate old proofs. Pin spec version; dual-verify during migration windows; silent mixed-version acceptance is a hole.

---

## D. Provenance/trust failure modes

**D1. Suffix laundering.** If the gate deep-verifies reused prefixes and rubber-stamps the "fresh" suffix, unvetted content hides in the suffix. Suffix spans carry their own provenance leaves (cheaper checks — fresh, single-source — but present). The suffix is never a provenance-free zone.

**D2. Lossy-node trust escalation.** Summaries are LLM-generated, nondeterministic, and injectable: a poisoned summary becomes a clean-looking anchor and persists across compactions. Derived nodes get a distinct, lower trust tier; they expire unless re-grounded against surviving raw sources within T turns. The gate validates lineage, not truth — anyone describing it as hallucination prevention is lying, and telemetry must not imply it.

**D3. Cross-principal contamination.** Shared prefix pools keyed by content hash leak across tenants: timing side channels, poisoned shared prefixes, and user B receiving summaries derived from user A's data. Checkpoints carry a provenance label = join of contributor labels; the gate enforces label ∩ requester-clearance ≠ ∅ on every reuse. No exceptions for "just the system prompt."

**D4. Provenance cycles via self-reading agents.** A tool that returns the conversation transcript makes the provenance DAG cyclic. Break it: the returned view is hashed as a new raw node flagged `contains-derivative`, not linked as its own ancestor.

**D5. Multi-hop facts.** Facts synthesized across two sources have no single parent. Span-level labels with multi-parent DAGs, or you force mislabeling. Coarse lineage ("derived from messages 0..k") fails citation audits; decide the granularity you commit to and honor it.

**D6. Wall-clock decisions.** Clock skew between writers and gate flaps TTL-based validity ("tool results older than X"). Order by chain-internal sequence numbers; timestamps advisory only.

---

## E. Performance/abuse boundaries

- **Anchor density:** first-class anchors require a minimum span (order 64–256 tokens); micro-edits coalesce; anchors capped per session. Otherwise adversarial many-tiny-turns contexts inflate memory and proof overhead (denial-of-wallet).
- **Giant immutable spans:** a 100k-token tool result with no internal boundary violates any suffix budget if anchors must respect safe-cut rules. Resolution: intra-span anchors permitted only for content-addressed immutable blobs — they cannot be edited underneath you, so interior cuts are safe.
- **Gate latency:** verdicts must land in µs–ms via the verdict cache; the deny path degrades to scheduled full re-prefill, never to skipping the gate, never to stalling decode past budget.

---

## Component boundaries (who guarantees what)

| Interface | Contract |
|---|---|
| Editor → Anchor mgr | Cut proposals are token-aligned, structurally safe, with exact edit-shape classification (append / middle / delete / replace) |
| Anchor mgr → KV store | Residency honored, pinning respected, refcount-correct page sharing under continuous batching (free on last unmap, never first) |
| KV store → Gate | Full checkpoint record (A5 field set) + residency bitmap; no partial segments |
| Chain → Gate | Pinned roots, incremental proofs, append-only leaves, tombstones |
| Gate → Scheduler | Fail-closed verdicts within latency budget; deny ⇒ honest recompute path |

## What must never happen (flat list)

1. KV reuse without matching `position_base`, model/adapter/kernel/rope versions.
2. Semantic-similarity or fuzzy match admitting KV reuse.
3. Byte-offset anchoring without token-boundary verification; accidental BOS duplication.
4. Partial KV segment reuse; in-place mutation under live decode.
5. Middle edits silently classified as suffix appends (without re-rotation or re-prefill).
6. Fail-open gate on any verification or infrastructure error.
7. Admission on content-hash match alone; sub-collision-resistant hash identifiers.
8. Cross-principal reuse without provenance-label intersection.
9. Lossy-derived (summary) nodes at raw-span trust tier, or persisting without re-grounding.
10. Suffix exempt from provenance checks.
11. In-place mutation of committed leaves; publishing roots referencing non-resident pages.
12. Bit-exact float fingerprint equality across independent compute runs.
13. Security/TTL decisions keyed to wall clock alone.
14. Checkpoint "hit" reported when fallback recompute occurred.
15. Index-keyed checkpoints without a concurrency resolution rule.
16. Treating checkpoint existence as sufficient for rollback revival (liveness re-check skipped).
17. Deletion of attention-sink head tokens by compaction.
18. The gate represented — in docs, dashboards, or claims — as validating semantic truth. It validates derivation lineage. Nothing more.
reasoning:
The user is asking about a hard systems problem: semantic-anchor checkpoints in a context-editing pipeline for an agent, where re-prefill only processes the new suffix of the context, integrated with a verkle chain (Verkle tree-based provenance chain) and a provenance gate. They want edge cases: failure modes, boundaries, and invariants ("what must never happen"). Concrete, exact, grounded.

Let me think about what this system actually is:

1. **Agent context editing**: An agent has a context window (prompt + history). When context is edited (truncation, summarization, compaction, tool-result eviction), you don't want to re-run prefill over the entire context — that's expensive. Instead, you want to reuse KV cache for the prefix and only prefill the new suffix.

2. **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: Checkpoints placed at "semantic anchors" — points where the context semantically changes or where it's safe to cut/reuse — e.g., message boundaries, tool-call boundaries, summary insertion points. Each anchor defines a prefix whose KV cache can be cached and reused. The checkpoint stores enough state (KV cache reference, token count, hash of prefix content) so that on edit, you find the longest matching anchor prefix and re-prefill only from there.

3. **Verkle chain / provenance gate**: A Verkle tree (vector commitment with small witness sizes) used as a provenance ledger. Every context state / checkpoint gets committed into a Verkle tree; edits append commitments; a "provenance gate" verifies that any suffix being prefilled traces back to committed, attested states — i.e., the gate checks that the KV cache you're about to reuse actually corresponds to a committed prefix hash, and that the new suffix's provenance (which documents/tools/summaries contributed tokens) is verifiable via Verkle witnesses without revealing everything.

So the composition: semantic-anchor checkpoints give you cache-reuse cut points; the Verkle chain gives tamper-evident provenance for each checkpoint and each token block; the provenance gate decides whether a proposed re-prefill (prefix reuse + suffix compute) is admissible.

Now I need edge cases. Let me enumerate systematically across layers:

**Layer A: Anchor placement & semantics**

1. **Anchor drift under summarization**: If a compaction step replaces messages [0..k] with a summary S, the old anchors inside [0..k] are dead. But the summary S itself may be generated nondeterministically (LLM call). Two runs produce different S → different hashes → anchor mismatch. Failure mode: cache miss at every anchor after compaction; worse, if you match by position rather than content, you'd reuse stale KV for a different semantic content — silent corruption. Must never happen: positional matching without content-hash verification.

2. **Anchor inside a logical unit**: Anchors must not be placed mid-tool-call (between tool_use and tool_result), mid-document (inside a quoted file chunk that later gets referenced by line number), or between a system-injected safety preamble and its dependent instructions. If an edit cuts at such an anchor, the suffix prefill sees a dangling tool_use or a half-quoted document. Failure mode: model hallucinates tool results or misattributes quotes. Boundary rule: anchors only at message/tool-roundtrip boundaries plus explicit "safe-cut" markers emitted by the editor.

3. **Duplicate prefixes / repeated boilerplate**: Agent contexts often repeat identical blocks (system prompt, few-shot examples, recurring tool schemas). Content-hash matching will match the *wrong* occurrence: longest-prefix match on hash chain could bind to an earlier duplicate rather than the intended one. If the two occurrences have different positions but same content, KV reuse is actually fine content-wise — unless positional encodings differ (RoPE offsets). This is a real failure mode: KV cache entries encode rotary position embeddings; reusing a prefix cached at offset 0 when the current prefix starts at offset 4096 produces wrong attention. Must never happen: KV reuse across different absolute position bases without re-rotation or recomputation. Concretely: store `base_position` in the checkpoint; verify `base_position` equality, not just content hash.

4. **Anchors too sparse/too dense**: Sparse anchors → large suffix re-prefill, cost blowup (the whole point was incremental). Dense anchors → memory blowup storing per-anchor KV references + Verkle proofs; also more gate checks per edit → latency. Boundary: anchor spacing policy must be bounded both ways, e.g., anchor every N tokens AND at every structural boundary, with N chosen so worst-case suffix ≤ some budget B. Edge case: a single huge tool result (100k tokens) with no internal boundary → forced either one giant anchor-free span (violating suffix budget) or artificial intra-document anchors (violating safe-cut rule). Resolution: intra-span anchors allowed only for immutable, content-addressed blobs (hash-committed), because they can't be edited underneath you.

**Layer B: Edit semantics & suffix computation**

5. **Non-suffix edits (middle insertions/deletions)**: The design assumes edits touch only the suffix. Real editors do middle insertions (inject a retrieved document at turn 12 of 30). Then "new suffix" is ill-defined: everything after the insertion point is unchanged textually but shifted positionally. Options: (a) full re-prefill from insertion point (correct, expensive); (b) position-shifted KV reuse (requires re-RoPE-ing all subsequent KV — O(n) work anyway, though cheaper than recompute since no MLP/FLOPs, just rotation math — this is real: rotating cached K/V vectors to new positions is linear and cheap relative to recompute); (c) refuse and fall back. Failure mode: naive systems treat middle-insert as suffix-append and reuse mismatched KV. Must never happen: silent acceptance of a middle edit as a suffix edit. The gate must compare the checkpoint's recorded prefix hash against the actual current prefix bytes; on mismatch, walk back to the previous anchor; if even anchor 0 mismatches, full re-prefill.

6. **Edit racing with generation**: An edit lands while the model is mid-decode using the old KV. If the editor swaps the cache under a live decode, attention reads torn state. Boundary: edits apply only at decode-step boundaries (between forward passes), and the swap must be atomic w.r.t. the running request — copy-on-write or double-buffer. Must never happen: in-place mutation of a KV segment referenced by an in-flight decode.

7. **Suffix boundary ambiguity — whitespace/tokenization seams**: Re-prefilling "only the new suffix" requires tokenizing the suffix independently. Tokenizers are context-dependent: BPE merges across the boundary (e.g., suffix begins mid-word, or a leading space/newline merges with prior token). If you tokenize the suffix standalone, you get different tokens than tokenizing the whole string. Failure mode: off-by-one token seam → subtly different meaning ("Hello world" vs "Hello" + " world" tokenizations differ). Rule: anchors must be placed at tokenizer-safe boundaries (token-aligned offsets verified by re-tokenizing prefix+first-token-of-suffix and checking stability), or the re-prefill window extends back to the last token-stable point. Must never happen: byte-offset anchoring without token-alignment verification.

8. **Cache eviction vs. anchor liveness**: KV cache is finite. Old anchors get evicted while still referenced by the Verkle chain as valid checkpoints. Gate says "reuse anchor k" but the KV pages are gone. Failure modes: (a) crash — unacceptable; (b) silently recompute from scratch but report "checkpoint hit" in telemetry — corrupts metrics and any billing/audit built on it; (c) worse: reuse *partially* evicted segments — garbage attention. Must never happen: partial-segment reuse. The gate must verify page-level residency (or a residency bitmap committed alongside the anchor) before admitting the reuse. Also: eviction policy must never evict an anchor that is the unique fallback for a live session below the last verified anchor — i.e., pinning rules.

9. **Determinism of the underlying model**: KV reuse assumes deterministic prefill: same tokens + same positions + same weights → same KV. Violations: (a) weight updates (fine-tuning, LoRA hot-swap) invalidate all caches — need a model-version field in the checkpoint, and the gate must check it; (b) non-deterministic kernels (atomics in fused attention, different batch shapes changing reduction order) cause tiny numeric drift — usually tolerable but breaks bit-exact replay claims; (c) sampling temperature doesn't matter for prefill but does for anything cached downstream. Edge case: quantized KV cache (fp8/int8) with dynamic scaling factors computed per-chunk — scale factors depend on neighboring chunks in the chunked quantization scheme, so a changed suffix changes scales of the *last prefix chunk*, meaning the true minimal re-prefill boundary is chunk-aligned, not token-aligned. Concrete: with chunked KV quant (chunk=128 tokens), reuse boundary must snap to 128-token grid or the last chunk's scales are wrong.

10. **Prefix hash collisions / truncation attacks**: If prefix identity is a truncated hash (e.g., 64-bit) to save space in the Verkle leaf, adversarial or accidental collision binds a checkpoint to wrong content. In a provenance-gated system, an attacker who can influence context content (tool results! web pages!) could grind a colliding prefix. Must never happen: sub-128-bit content identifiers admitted by the gate; use full 256-bit hashes; the Verkle key derivation should include the hash domain-separated from position index.

**Layer C: Verkle chain specifics**

11. **Witness staleness / chain reorg**: If the provenance chain is maintained as an append-only Verkle tree with periodic root publication, and roots are gossiped, a lagging validator holds an old root; new checkpoints prove against a newer root it doesn't know. Failure mode: gate rejects valid checkpoints (availability failure) or, if the system auto-updates roots without verification, accepts forged ones. Boundary: root updates require signature verification against a pinned key set; rejection must trigger catch-up, not bypass. Must never happen: "fail-open" gate behavior on root fetch errors.

12. **Insertion order dependence in Verkle keys**: Verkle trees commit to a key→value map. If checkpoint keys are sequential indices, a fork/race in checkpoint creation (two workers create anchor k+1 concurrently from different suffixes) creates a conflict. Resolution rules needed: content-addressed keys (hash(prefix)) make inserts idempotent and order-independent; index keys make them conflicting. Edge case: same content reaching anchor k+1 via two different paths (e.g., two identical tool results inserted in different orders producing same final context) — content-addressing dedupes correctly; index-addressing forks. Prefer content addressing; then handle the pathological case of hash collision (see #10).

13. **Proof size vs. gate latency**: Verkle witnesses are small (~a few hundred bytes to KBs) but verifying per-token-block proofs on a hot path adds latency. If the gate verifies a proof per anchor per edit, and edits are frequent (every turn), verification cost compounds. Boundary: amortize — verify the chain incrementally (each new checkpoint's proof links to previously verified root), so per-edit cost is O(1) verifications, not O(depth). Failure mode: naive implementation re-verifies from genesis each time → quadratic behavior over long sessions. Must never happen: unbounded re-verification growth; also must never skip verification because "we verified this root before" without caching the verified-root set keyed by root hash + epoch.

14. **What exactly is committed?** Subtle and critical: commit the *content hash* of the prefix, or the *KV cache fingerprint*? These can diverge: same content, different KV (different quantization run, different kernel version) — content matches but KV differs; or (theoretically) same KV fingerprint, different content (collision). The gate's job is provenance: "this KV state derives from these committed contents." So the checkpoint record must bind {model_version, tokenizer_version, content_hash, position_base, kv_fingerprint, quant_params}. Failure mode: committing only content_hash lets a stale/mismatched KV pass the gate after a kernel upgrade. Must never happen: gate admission on content match alone.

15. **Pruning vs. auditability**: Verkle chains allow compact state, but provenance gates sometimes need historical witnesses ("prove this answer cited document D as it existed at time t"). If checkpoints prune old values on update (in-place Verkle value overwrite), history is lost. Boundary: values must be append-only (versioned leaves: key = H(content, seq)), with a separate pruning policy for storage, never for the commitment structure. Must never happen: overwriting a committed leaf value in place — that breaks reproducibility of past gate decisions.

16. **Cross-session/cross-tenant leakage via shared anchors**: Identical prefixes across users (same system prompt) tempt shared KV pools keyed by content hash. Provenance-wise fine, but: (a) side channels (timing differences reveal whether another tenant warmed your prefix); (b) poisoning — one tenant's tool results embedded in a "shared" prefix propagate; (c) access-control: the gate must enforce that a reused prefix's provenance set is readable/admissible for the requesting principal. Failure mode: user B's context includes a summary derived from user A's data because the anchor pool matched on content. Must never happen: cross-principal KV reuse without a provenance-permission check on every contributing source. Concretely: the checkpoint carries a provenance label = join of source labels; gate computes label intersection with requester's clearance.

17. **Summary/provenance compression loses token-level linkage**: After compaction, the summary's provenance is "derived from messages 0..k," but the gate may need finer granularity (which sentence came from which doc) for citation audits. If the Verkle leaf only stores coarse lineage, post-hoc audits fail. Edge case: a hallucinated detail in the summary — provenance gate can't detect it (it validates lineage, not truthfulness). Boundary statement: the gate proves derivation integrity, not semantic correctness; anything claiming otherwise is a design lie. What must never happen: marketing/telemetry describing the gate as preventing hallucination.

18. **Re-prefill nondeterminism vs. committed expectations**: Suppose the system commits an expected KV fingerprint at checkpoint creation, then later re-prefills the same span (cache evicted) and compares. Kernel nondeterminism (#9b) makes fingerprints mismatch → false invalidation storms. Boundary: fingerprint comparison needs tolerance bands (per-channel max-abs-diff thresholds) or fingerprint over quantized buckets only. Must never happen: hard equality on float fingerprints across independent compute runs.

19. **Gate bypass via suffix laundering**: Attack: put questionable content in the "suffix" region, claiming it's newly generated and thus exempt from prefix provenance checks. If the gate only deeply verifies reused prefixes and rubber-stamps suffixes, an agent can smuggle unvetted content (e.g., injected tool output) into the suffix. Rule: suffix tokens still carry their own provenance leaves (source-tagged spans); the gate verifies suffix span proofs too, just with cheaper checks (they're fresh, single-source). Must never happen: suffix treated as provenance-free zone.

20. **Checkpoint creation itself is an LLM call (summaries)**: The summary generator is nondeterministic and potentially manipulable (prompt injection in summarized content alters future behavior — classic). The Verkle chain faithfully records a poisoned summary. Provenance gate passes it because lineage is intact. Failure mode: persistence of injection across compactions — the summary becomes a trusted-looking anchor. Mitigations: summaries must be marked derived-with-lossy-provenance; downstream gates treat lossy nodes as lower trust; optionally re-verify summary against sources with an extractor. Must never happen: a lossy-derived node granted the same trust tier as raw committed spans.

21. **Time/ordering anomalies**: Clock skew between the writer appending checkpoints and the gate validating — if leaves embed timestamps used for TTL decisions (e.g., "tool results older than X are stale"), skew causes flapping validity. Use chain-internal sequence numbers for ordering; timestamps only advisory. Must never happen: security decisions keyed to wall-clock alone.

22. **Partial writes / crash consistency**: Writer appends checkpoint to Verkle tree, then persists KV pages, crashes between. Now chain says anchor exists; storage lacks pages. Recovery must reconcile: on startup, scan chain tips vs. residency bitmap, mark orphaned checkpoints invalid (tombstone), never trust chain-alone. Conversely: pages persisted before chain append → orphan pages, harmless but wasteful; ordering should be write-pages → fsync → append-chain → publish root. Must never happen: publishing a root that references non-resident pages (that's the crash-window hazard).

23. **Token-level provenance vs. attention reality**: Claim: "this output token attended mostly to source S." Any gating that relies on attention attribution is fragile — attention weights are not faithful explanations; also with KV reuse, the suffix attends to prefix KV whose provenance is aggregate. Edge case: a fact synthesized across two sources (multi-hop) has no single-source provenance; forcing single-source labels causes mislabeling. Boundary: provenance labels at span level with multi-parent DAGs, not single-parent.

24. **Long-context position overflow**: Context grows; RoPE base or YaRN scaling changes mid-session (config bump) → all cached KV invalid. Model_version must include rope config hash. Trivially stated, commonly missed.

25. **Empty/degenerate suffixes**: Edit that deletes everything after anchor k → suffix empty → no prefill needed, but decode still needs a next-token distribution; ensure the "no-op prefill" path still emits correct logits from cached final position, including updating any sliding-window attention bookkeeping. Edge case: models with sliding-window attention (Mistral-style) — KV beyond window is dropped; anchors older than window are unusable regardless of residency; gate must model the attention architecture's effective horizon, else admits reuse that the model can't actually perform. Must never happen: gate logic ignorant of attention-type constraints (full vs. sliding vs. sinking vs. hybrid).

26. **Batching interactions**: Continuous batching: multiple requests share a physical KV pool; page tables (vLLM-style PagedAttention) map logical→physical. Anchor reuse across requests means sharing physical pages — refcounting bugs → one request's eviction frees pages another uses. Must never happen: refcount underflow; free-on-first-unmap instead of last.

27. **The "longest match" greedy trap**: Longest-prefix-match picks the deepest anchor whose hash matches. But suppose anchor k matches content yet its KV was created under a different *suffix-independent* condition that matters — e.g., a "contextual soft prompt" or per-request system steering vector active at original prefill but absent now. Content hash can't see it. Checkpoint record must include all conditioning inputs (adapters, steering, sampling-config irrelevant but adapter-relevant). Failure mode: subtle behavior shift attributed to "model mood."

28. **Verkle key namespace exhaustion / migration**: If key schema version bumps (v1→v2 layout), old proofs don't verify under new spec. Gates must pin spec version; migration must dual-verify during transition windows. Must never happen: mixed-version verification accepted silently.

29. **Denial-of-wallet via anchor inflation**: Adversary crafts contexts maximizing anchor count (many tiny turns) → memory + proof overhead per session explodes. Rate-limit anchors per session; coalesce micro-spans. Boundary: minimum span length for a first-class anchor; smaller spans fold into parent.

30. **Rollback semantics**: User hits "undo" reverting context to earlier state. Chain is append-only; rollback = new forward pointer to old checkpoint. Fine — but any *invalidations* that happened meanwhile (e.g., a source document revoked/tombstoned in provenance store) mean the rolled-back-to state is no longer admissible even though the checkpoint exists. True semantic anchoring would allow matching paraphrases (summary rewritten slightly) — but that's unsound for KV reuse (different tokens = different KV, period). So the sound design: semantic anchors determine *where* cuts are legal (structural/semantic units), while *reuse* eligibility is strictly syntactic (exact token match + position + model match).
